Headline: TGME49_215490 encodes the T.gondii essential arginine plamsa membrane transporter
Content: The transporter protein encoded by TGME49_215490 is the essential arginine plasma membrane transporter in T.gondii. The transporter is a member of the Major Facilitator Superfamily of membrane transporters, or solute carriers, and is a net accumulator of arginine both in vivo and in vitro, which is essential for parasite survival and which the parasite cannot synthesis (see PMID: 28205520,  DOI: 10.1038/ncomms14455). This transporter has been renamed ApiAT1 (Apicomplexan Amino acid Transporter 1) and forms one of 16 members in T.gondii (5 in Plasmodium species), several others of which have also been characterised as amino acid or amino acid metabolite transporters and several of which are essential for correct growth of the parasite in the tachyzoite stage (PMID: 30742695,  DOI: 10.1371/journal.ppat.1007577). Within MFS, the ApiAT form part of a family that has closest homology to the SLC43 (Solute Carrier 43) family in Homo sapiens, also known as the L-Amino Acid Transporter-3 (LAT3) Family or in the TCDB (Transporter Classification Database) as family 2.A.1.44 and PF07690 in the Pfam Protein fold database. The transporter is essential for parasite virulence when examined in mice infected with T.gondii. ApiAT1 is also the closest ortholog to Plasmodium berghei ApiAT1 (PbApiAT1), which was also shown to be a cationic amino acid transporter (see PMID: 28205520,  DOI: 10.1038/ncomms14455) and causes defects in gametocyte development and with progression into the insect stages of the Plasmodium life cycle when knocked out (PMID: 21752110 DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-2958.2011.07767.x).
PubMed Titles: The novel putative transporter NPT1 plays a critical role in early stages of Plasmodium berghei sexual development. | Cationic amino acid transporters play key roles in the survival and transmission of apicomplexan parasites. | The tyrosine transporter of Toxoplasma gondii is a member of the newly defined apicomplexan amino acid transporter (ApiAT) family.

Headline: IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH) cloning and characterization
Content: The opportunistic apicomplexan parasite Toxoplasma gondii damages fetuses in utero and threatens immunocompromised individuals. The toxicity associated with standard antitoxoplasmal therapies, which target the folate pathway, underscores the importance of examining alternative pharmacological strategies. Parasitic protozoa cannot synthesize purines de novo; consequently, targeting purine salvage enzymes is a plausible pharmacological strategy. Several enzymes critical to purine metabolism have been studied in T. gondii, but IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH), which catalyzes the conversion of IMP to XMP, has yet to be characterized. Thus, we have cloned the gene encoding this enzyme in T. gondii. Northern blot analysis shows that two IMPDH transcripts are present in T. gondii tachyzoites. The larger transcript contains an open reading frame of 1,656 nucleotides whose deduced protein sequence consists of 551 amino acids (TgIMPDH). The shorter transcript is an alternative splice product that generates a 371-amino-acid protein lacking the active-site flap (TgIMPDH-S). When TgIMPDH is expressed as a recombinant protein fused to a FLAG tag, the fusion protein localizes to the parasite cytoplasm. Immunoprecipitation with anti-FLAG was employed to purify recombinant TgIMPDH, which converts IMP to XMP as expected. Mycophenolic acid is an uncompetitive inhibitor relative to NAD+, with a intercept inhibition constant (Kii) of 0.03+/-0.004 microM. Tiazofurin and its seleno analog were not inhibitory to the purified enzyme, but adenine dinucleotide analogs such as TAD and the nonhydrolyzable beta-methylene derivatives of TAD or SAD were inhibitory, with Kii values 13- to 60-fold higher than that of mycophenolic acid.
PubMed Titles: IMP dehydrogenase from the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii.

Headline: MIC8
Content:
Gene Name: MIC8
Function: invasion, rhoptry secretion
Synonyms: TgMIC8, Microneme protein 8
Cellular Location: Micronemes
 
Comment: TGME49_045490 gene model is an incorrect fusion of TgMIC8 and TgMIC9, which are tandemly arranged. TgMIC8 is a 70 kDa type I transmembrane protein with one chitin binding like (CBL) domain and 10 EGF domains in its luminal region. Binds to TgMIC3 but is not necessary to escort TgMIC3 to the micronemes. Conditional knockout parasites have an invasion defect probably due to an inability to secrete rhoptries and form a moving junction. The C-terminal cytosolic domain is essential for its function. Proposed to play a role in signalling for rhoptry discharge. Not necessary for gliding motility or egress.

Interacts with: TGME49_119560
PubMed Titles: Microneme protein 8--a new essential invasion factor in Toxoplasma gondii. | A family of transmembrane microneme proteins of Toxoplasma gondii contain EGF-like domains and function as escorters.
PubMed Authors: Kessler et al. | Meissner et al.

Headline: TgVP1 localizes to the Plant-like Vacuole
Content:

It has been shown to acidify the PLV through its proton pumping activity. During extracellular stages, VP1 colocalizes with TgCPL and TgAQP1 in the PLV. This localization is lost immediately after host cell invasion and TgVP1 becomes associated with Rab7-labeled late endosomes.

Headline: Clusters with NTE-containing clade of ROPKs
Content:
Clusters phylogenetically with ROP2, ROP8 and (most closely) ROP5, which have been shown in structural studies to contain an unique, rhoptry-kinase-specific amino-terminal extension (NTE) to the kinase domain which stabilizes the N-lobe of the kinase fold. See Labesse 2009, Qiu 2009, Reese 2011. Sequence alignment of ROP24 with these NTE-containing proteins suggests the N-terminal flank of the ROP24 kinase domain shares homology and therefore also appears to contain this NTE segment.

The NTE region is adjacent to the kinase domain, not to be confused with the series of membrane-binding amphipathic helices (RAH domains, per Reese 2009) further in the N-tail, which ROP24 also contains (permitting association with the PVM, per Peixoto 2010).

Headline: GCN5-A functions in the cellular response to alkaline stress and expression of cyst genes
Content: Parasitic protozoa such as the apicomplexan Toxoplasma gondii progress through their life cycle in response to stimuli in the environment or host organism. Very little is known about how proliferating tachyzoites reprogram their expressed genome in response to stresses that prompt development into latent bradyzoite cysts. We have previously linked histone acetylation with the expression of stage-specific genes, but the factors involved remain to be determined. We sought to determine if GCN5, which operates as a transcriptional co-activator by virtue of its histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity, contributed to stress-induced changes in gene expression in Toxoplasma. In contrast to other lower eukaryotes, Toxoplasma has duplicated its GCN5 lysine acetyltransferase (KAT). Disruption of the gene encoding for TgGCN5-A in type I RH strain did not produce a severe phenotype under normal culture conditions, but here we show that the TgGCN5-A null mutant is deficient in responding to alkaline pH, a common stress used to induce bradyzoite differentiation in vitro. We performed a genome-wide analysis of the Toxoplasma transcriptional response to alkaline pH stress, finding that parasites deleted for TgGCN5-A fail to up-regulate 74% of the stress response genes that are induced 2-fold or more in wild-type. Using chromatin immunoprecipitation, we verify an enrichment of TgGCN5-A at the upstream regions of genes activated by alkaline pH exposure. The TgGCN5-A knockout is also incapable of up-regulating key marker genes expressed during development of the latent cyst form, and is impaired in its ability to recover from alkaline stress. Complementation of the TgGCN5-A knockout restores the expression of these stress-induced genes and reverses the stress recovery defect. These results establish TgGCN5-A as a major contributor to the alkaline stress response in RH strain Toxoplasma.
PubMed Titles: Toxoplasma gondii lysine acetyltransferase GCN5-A functions in the cellular response to alkaline stress and expression of cyst genes.

Headline: TgPuf1
Content:
Background
Puf proteins act as translational regulators and affect many cellular processes in a wide range of eukaryotic organisms. Although Puf proteins have been well characterized in many model systems, little is known about the structural and functional characteristics of Puf proteins in the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. 

Methods
Using a combination of conventional molecular approaches, we generated endogenous TgPuf1 tagged with hemagglutinin (HA) epitope and investigated the TgPuf1 expression levels and localization in the tachyzoites and bradyzoites. We used RNA Electrophoretic Mobility Shfit Assay (EMSA) to determine whether the recombination TgPuf1 has conserverd RNA binding activity and specificity. 

Results
TgPuf1 was expressed at a significantly higher level in bradyzoites than in tachyzoites. TgPuf1 protein was predominantly localized within the cytoplasm and showed a much more granular cytoplasmic staining pattern in bradyzoites. The recombinant Puf domain of TgPuf1 showed strong binding affinity to two RNA fragments containing Puf-binding motifs from other organisms as artificial target sequences. However, two point mutations in the core Puf-binding motif resulted in a significant reduction in binding affinity, indicating that TgPuf1 also binds to conserved Puf-binding motif. 

Conclusions
TgPuf1 appears to exhibit different expression levels in the tachyzoites and bradyzoites, suggesting that TgPuf1 may function in regulating the proliferation or/and differentiation that are important in providing parasites with the ability to respond rapidly to changes in environmental conditions. This study provides a starting point for elucidating the function of TgPuf1 during parasite development.
PubMed Titles: Characterization of TgPuf1, a member of the Puf family RNA-binding proteins from Toxoplasma gondii.

Headline: Repeated secondary loss of adaptin complex genes in the Apicomplexa.
Content:
Parasitol Int. 2009 Mar;58(1):86-94. Epub 2008 Dec 24.
Repeated secondary loss of adaptin complex genes in the Apicomplexa.
Nevin WD, Dacks JB.

Abstract

The Apicomplexa include parasites of devastating medical and economic consequence. While obviously essential for their parasitic mechanism, the molecular machinery underpinning membrane-trafficking in many apicomplexans is poorly understood. One potentially key set of players, the adaptins, selects cargo for incorporation into trafficking vesicles. Four distinct adaptin (AP) complexes exist in eukaryotes; AP1 and AP3 are involved in transport between the trans-Golgi Network (TGN) and endosomes, AP4 in TGN to cell surface transport, and AP2 in endocytosis from the cell surface. Of particular interest is the involvement of AP1 in Toxoplasma rhoptry biogenesis. The recent completion of several apicomplexan genomes should jump-start molecular parasitological studies and provide systems-level insight into the apicomplexan adaptin machinery. However, many of the encoded adaptin proteins are annotated conservatively and not to the necessary complex or subunit level. Prompted by previous evidence suggesting the lack of AP3 in Plasmodium falciparum, we undertook homology-searching and phylogenetic analysis to produce a rigorously annotated set of adaptin subunits encoded in diverse apicomplexan genomes. We found multiple losses of adaptins across the phylum; in particular Theileria, Babesia, and Cryptosporidium, but surprisingly not Plasmodium, appear to have lost the entirety of the AP3 complex. The losses correlate with a degenerate Golgi body structure and are reminiscent of recently reported secondary losses of additional endocytic components (i.e. the ESCRTs) in several Apicomplexa. These data may indicate a relaxation of the selective pressure on the apicomplexan endocytic system and, regardless, should greatly facilitate future molecular cell biological investigation of the role of adaptins in these important parasites.

Headline: TgIF2K-D is a GCN2-like eukaryotic initiation factor 2 kinase that increases the viability of extracellular parasites
Content: Toxoplasmosis is a significant opportunistic infection caused by the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular pathogen that relies on host cell nutrients for parasite proliferation. Toxoplasma parasites divide until they rupture the host cell, at which point the extracellular parasites must survive until they find a new host cell. Recent studies have indicated that phosphorylation of Toxoplasma eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2-alpha (TgIF2α) plays a key role in promoting parasite viability during times of extracellular stress. Here we report the cloning and characterization of a TgIF2α kinase designated TgIF2K-D that is related to GCN2, a eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α) kinase known to respond to nutrient starvation in other organisms. TgIF2K-D is present in the cytosol of both intra- and extracellular Toxoplasma parasites and facilitates translational control through TgIF2α phosphorylation in extracellular parasites. We generated a TgIF2K-D knockout parasite and demonstrated that loss of this eIF2α kinase leads to a significant fitness defect that stems from an inability of the parasite to adequately adapt to the environment outside host cells. This phenotype is consistent with that reported for our nonphosphorylatable TgIF2α mutant (S71A substitution), establishing that TgIF2K-D is the primary eIF2α kinase responsible for promoting extracellular viability of Toxoplasma. These studies suggest that eIF2α phosphorylation and translational control are an important mechanism by which vulnerable extracellular parasites protect themselves while searching for a new host cell. Additionally, TgIF2α is phosphorylated when intracellular parasites are deprived of nutrients, but this can occur independently of TgIF2K-D, indicating that this activity can be mediated by a different TgIF2K.
PubMed Titles: A GCN2-like eukaryotic initiation factor 2 kinase increases the viability of extracellular Toxoplasma gondii parasites.

Headline: ICMAP3 - two isoforms
Content: ICMAP3 (TGME49_500200) is coding for two isoforms: a short isoform called ICMAP3I (previously known as TGME49_285150) and a long isoform called ICMAP3II (previously spanning both TGME49_285150 and TGME49_285140 gene models). By plaque assay, conditional depletion of ICMAP3I is fitness conferring (but not essential) while depletion of ICMAP3II has no effect on the parasite fitness. By U-ExM, ICMAP3I localizes along the length of the intraconoidal microtubules (ICMTs) while ICMAP3II only localizes to the ICMTs lower part. Cryo-ET revealed that ICMAP3I is involved in the docking of the rhoptries with the AV, while ICMAP3II is mostly involved in the control of the ICMTs length. Conditional depletion of ICMAP3I leads do a defect in rhoptry discharge.
PubMed Titles: Sustained rhoptry docking and discharge requires Toxoplasma gondii intraconoidal microtubule-associated proteins.

Headline: The glycosomal L-gulonolactone oxidase is a D-arabinonolactone oxidase
Content:
L-gulonolactone oxidase
The enzyme catalyzes the reaction of  L-galactono-1,4-lactone with dioxygen to produce L-xylohexulonolactone and hydrogen peroxide. The product spontaneously isomerizes to L-ascorbate. The enzyme is absent from humans, who need vitamin C, making it a potential drug target. Alignment and subsequent tree construction of the three tritryp sequences with the mammalian gulonolactone oxidases and the yeast D-arabinonolactone oxidase shows that they are all related enzymes belonging to one family. Wilkinson et al. (PMID: 17627608) have shown that this enzyme in T. cruzi  and in T. brucei functions as a D-arabinono-lactone oxidase similar to the situation in yeast. The presence of an arabinose dehydrogenase or aldo/ketose reductase (LmjF31.2150 in Leishmania) suggests that the yeast pathway of synthesis of erythroascorbate rather than ascorbate itself, is operational in trypanosomatids. It is not yet clear how the arabinose can be formed. Interestingly the homologues in T. brucei  and T. cruzi carry a PTS1. See also Opperdoes and Coombs, 2007; PMID:17320480

Headline: ERBP1

Loss of ERBP1 from bloodstream-form T. brucei initially resulted in a growth defect but proliferation was restored after more prolonged cultivation. Results from a pull-down of tagged ERBP1 suggest that it preferentially binds to ribosomal protein mRNAs. The ERBP1 sequence resembles that of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Bfr1, which also localises to the endoplasmic reticulum and binds to ribosomal protein mRNAs. However, unlike Bfr1, ERBP1 does not bind to mRNAs encoding secreted proteins, and it is also not recruited to stress granules after starvation.

Headline: Adenylate cyclase (ESAG4 / GRESAG4)
Content: T. brucei possesses a large family of bloodstream stage-specific transmembrane receptor-like adenylate cyclases (Rolin et al., 1990; PMID: 2209793) in about 58 copies. While many ESAG4s (for expression site associated gene 4) are located in the VSG expression sites (ES), the majority, termed genes related to ESAG4 (GRESAG4s), are not encoded in ESs and are expressed constitutively throughout the life cycle. ESAG 4-related glycoproteins are present only at the surface of the flagellum (Paindavoine et al., 1992; PMID: 1545803). Their function is the inhibition of the innate immune response of the host (Salmon et al., 2012;PMID: 22700656). Activation of these enzymes requires the dimerization of the catalytic domain. Internalization of adenylate cyclase by liver myeloid cells through phagocytosis inhibits the synthesis of TNFα (tumor necrosis factor-α) in the host cells through activation of protein kinase A. Thus, adenylate cyclase activity of lysed trypanosomes favors early host colonization by live parasites. This role of adenylate cyclases could be the explanation for the expansion and polymorphism of this gene family.

Headline: Alanine aminotransferase (AAT, Tb927.1.3950)
Content: The enzyme is present in all stages and has been used as a marker for the cytosol in subcellular fractionation studies of T. brucei (Steiger et al., 1980;PMID:6245876). The enzyme is abundantly present in both bloodstream and procyclic stages. More than 95% of the activity appears to be unnecessary for growth of either stage respiring on glucose. However, the enzyme has an important role in procyclic forms respiring on proline. Enzymes involved in the catabolism of proline are: proline dehydrogenase, 2-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, succinate dehydrogenase, fumarase, malate dehydrogenase, NADP-linked malic enzyme and alanine aminotransferase. A major end product of proline metabolism is alanine, reduction in TbAAT activity by RNAi led to a proportionate decrease in the amount of alanine excreted along with an increase in the doubling time of the cells (Spitznagel et al., 2009; PMID: 19895576)

Headline: Pyruvate dehydrogenase
Content: This multi-enzyme complex consists of four different subunits E1 alpha, E1 beta, E2 and E3. E1 (the actual pyruvate dehydrogenase) is a heterodimer of alpha subunits (Tb927.10.12700) and beta subunits (Tb927.3.1790). E2 is a dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase E2 subunit (Tb927.10.7570) and E3 is a dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (Tb11.01.8470). The enzyme is not expressed in the long slender stage, but is expressed in  procyclics and in short stumpy trypanosomes (Flynn and Bowman 1970; 1973; PMID: 5442050,PMID:4719992). E2 also functions as mitochondrial inheritance factor necessary for the distribution of kDNA networks to daughter cells at cytokinesis and is also expressed in bloodstream forms (Sykes and Hajduk, 2013; PMID:23125353).
PubMed Titles: Dual functions of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase E2 in the Krebs cycle and mitochondrial DNA inheritance in Trypanosoma brucei. | Comparative biochemistry of monomorphic and pleomorphic strains of Trypanosoma rhodesiense. | The metabolism of carbohydrate by pleomorphic African trypanosomes.

Headline: aka UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase
Content:
UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase
the enzyme catalyses the formation of UDP-glucose from glucose-1-phosphate and UTP. This activation step enables glucose to enter metabolic pathways and is crucial for the activation of galactose since galactokinase is absent. UDP-galactose is made from UDP-glucose by nucleotide-donor transfer to galactose-1-phosphate or by epimerisation of the glucose moiety. The latter reaction occurs inside glycosomes. The enzym is involved both in anabolic and catabolic pathways and therefore is an interesting drug target.
The pathway is: Glc --> glc6P --> glc1P -->UDP-Glc --> UDP-gal
For the other pathway via galactose-1-P the uridyl phosphotransferase does not seem to be operational in trypanosomes. Also phosphoglucomutase has not been identified in T. brucei and its activity has been taken over by the enzymes phospho-N-acetylglucosamine mutase (PAGM) and phosphomannomutase (PMM) (Bandini et al., 2012 PMID:22676716)
The enzyme has been expressed and characterized and the crystal structure has been solved : Marino et al., 2010; PMID:20724435
PubMed Titles: Identification, subcellular localization, biochemical properties, and high-resolution crystal structure of Trypanosoma brucei UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase. | Phosphoglucomutase is absent in Trypanosoma brucei and redundantly substituted by phosphomannomutase and phospho-N-acetylglucosamine mutase.

Headline: One aconitase with two intracellular locations
Content:
Aconitase
T. brucei aconitase gene is closely related to mammalian iron-regulatory protein 1 (IRP-1) and plant aconitases. The enzyme has been cloned sequenced and charaterized by Saas et al., 2000; PMID:10644738). The enzyme is differentially regulated, lowest in the slender bloodstream stage of the parasite, 8-fold elevated in the stumpy stage, and increased a further 4-fold in the procyclic stage. Contrary to animal cells who have two isoenzymes, T. brucei has only one, which localizes to both the mitochondrion (30%) and the cytoplasm (70%). Knock out of the aconitase gene in procyclic cells did not reveal any phenotype (Van Weelden et al 2003;PMID: 12562769).

Headline: Composition of the F1F0 ATPase
Content:
F1Fo-ATPase or ATP synthase.
The ATP synthase (or F1Fo-ATPase, or the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex V) consists of two major components, the soluble, catalytic F1 moiety and the membrane bound, proton pore Fo moiety. The Escherichia coli F1 moiety consists of five subunits in a stoichiometry of (α3β3γ1δ1ε1), and the Fo consists of the three subunits in a stoichiometry of a1b2c10¿14 [Devenish et al., 2008; PMID:18544496]. While the F1 structure is conserved, the number of Fo subunits varies among organisms and in mammalian systems there are at least 7 additional subunits beyond the core bacterial components (defg(A6L)F6 and OSCP or oligomycin-sensitivity conferring protein) [Devenish et al., 2008; PMID:18544496; Baker et al., 2012;PMID:22753497]. Most of the subunits of the eukaryotic ATP synthases are encoded in the nucleus with the exception of subunits a (aka 6), 8, and in some cases, subunit c (aka 9) [Devenish et al., 2008; PMID:18544496]. 

The F1 moiety in T. brucei is also comprised of the five core subunits, while its Fo moiety is believed to be similar in complexity to those found in other eukaryotic organisms [Zikova et al., 2009 PMID:19436713], [Williams and Frank, 1990, PMID:2149743]. In addition to subunit o or OSCP and c (or DCCD-binding protein) a total of 22 subunits are believed to be present in the complex (of which 14 are unique to T. brucei) [Zikova et al., 2009 PMID:19436713](see below). 
In T. brucei there are two tandemly linked 100% identical F1-ATPase alpha subunits (Tb927.7.7420 and Tb927.7.7430). This subunit is nuclear-encoded and carries a mitochondrial targeting signal. The alpha subunit is not only involved in ATP synthesis, but also in tRNA import in mitochondria and in RNA editing. In the latter case the ATPase alpha subunit undergoes a cleavage [Nelson et al., 2004; PMID:15110463; Goswami et al. 2006; PMID:16714384 and Goswami et al., 2006;PMID:16825195].Other subunits are beta (Tb927.3.1380), gamma (Tb10.100.0070) and epsilon (Tb927.6.4990). T. brucei has 3 subunit c (aka subunit 9) isoforms c-1, c-2, and c-3 (Tb11.02.2950, Tb927.10.1570) and Tb927.7.1470)(Gulde et al., 2013; PMID:23326569).It has one OSCP or subunit o (Tb927.10.8030), one subunit delta (Tb927.6.4990, annotated as epsilon in GeneDB) [Zikova et al., 2009 PMID:19436713] and one subunit epsilon (Tb927.10.5050). An additional subunit a (aka subunit 6 or MURF4, P24499) is encoded by the mitochondrial maxi circle. In procyclic insect stages the F1 ATPase is involved in the mitochondrial synthesis of ATP, using the mitochondrial transmembrane proton gradient, while in bloodstream forms the enzyme functions in the reverse direction and ATP is consumed and used for the creation of such a proton gradient. A mutation in the gamma subunit of F1-ATPase in the dyskinetoplastic form is likely to be involved in facilitating this reversal in the absence of the mitochondrially encoded subunit [Schnaufer et al., 2005;PMID:16270030].Interestingly OSCP and DCCD-binding proteis in mammals are encoded by the mitochondrial genome, while in T. brucei they are nuclear-encoded. Only subunit a (see above) has been identified as mitochondrially encoded.

Headline: IMPDH1 and IMPDH2 which may be a GMP reductase
Content:
Inosine-monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH)
In T. brucei there are two IMPDH genes impdh1 (Tb927.10.16120) and impdh2 (Tb927.5.2080). They encode homologous proteins of similar size. Both predicted isoenzymes have a PTS1 (-SKL and -AKL, respectively). The presence of IMPDH1 has been confirmed by proteomic analysis: It is present in glycosomes, and expressed in both life-cycle stage with the highest abundance in the bloodstream stage (Vertommen et al., 2007; PMID:18242729). Orthologues of these two homologous genes are present in all trypanosomatids.  They differ by about 66% at the protein level. The Tb927.10.16120 predicted protein sequence is incomplete. It starts from a downstream initiation codon. Tb927.10.16120 is of true eukaryotic origin, while Tb927.5.2080 is a bacterial type of sequence. The annotation of Tb927.5.2080 has been changed into a "GMP reductase" since TriTrypDB version 4!  The T. brucei IMPDH1 isoenzyme has been overexpressed and characterized (Bessho et al., 2013;PMID:23369253). A crystal structure of the human enzyme is available (pdb|1JCN).

Headline: homologous to IMPDH and 66% different at the protein level
Content: Tb927.5.2080 was originally annotated as an inosine-monophosphate dehydrogenase, but it was not clear why there should be two glycosomal IMPDHs (Tb927.5.2080 and Tb927.10.16120, while an other glycosomal enzyme (GMP synthase) responsible for the conversion of GMP into IMP was apparently missing (Vertommen et al., 2007; PMID:18242729). Since TriTrypDB version 4 IMPDH (Tb927.5.2080) became a GMP reductase, and although this could eaqually be correct it needs experimental confirmation. GMPR catalyzes the irreversible and NADPH-dependent reductive deamination of GMP to IMP, and plays a critical role in re-utilization of free intracellular bases and purine nucleosides. Tb927.5.2080 is of bacterial descent and Tb927.10.16120 of eukaryotic descent. They are homologous enzymes of similar lengths. Phylogenetic analysis does not give a clear-cut picture , nor does analysis via IPRScan. A leishmania GMP reductase has been purified and characterized. It is very sensitive to inhibition by allopurinol nucleotides (Spector and Jones 1982;PMID:7159467). See also IMPDH, Tb927.10.16120.

Headline: G6PDH, the first enzyme of the pentose-phosphate shunt
Content:
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
This is the first enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway. Both bloodstream forms and procyclic insect stages contain glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.49), 6-phosphogluconolactonase (EC 3.1.1.31), 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.44), ribose-5-phosphate isomerase (EC 5.3.1.6) and transaldolase (EC 2.2.1.2). However, ribulose-5-phosphate 3'-epimerase (EC 5.1.3.1) and transketolase (EC 2.2.1.1) activities are detectable only in procyclic forms (Cronin et al, 1989, PMID:2924907).

Headline: G6PDH as a drug target
Content: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH, TB10.70.5200), the first enzyme of the pentosephosphate pathway, is essential for the defense of the parasite against oxidative stress. Trypanosomatid G6PDHs contain a unique 37 amino acid long N-terminal extension that in T. cruzi seems to regulate the enzyme activity in a redox-state-dependent manner (Gupta et al. 20011;PMID:22091394). T. brucei and T. cruzi G6PDHs, but not their Leishmania spp. counterpart, are inhibited, in an uncompetitive way, by steroids such as dehydroepiandrosterone and derivatives (Cordeiro et al, 2009: PMID:19231202; Gupta et al., 2011; PMID:22091394; PMID:21185333). The Trypanosoma enzymes are more susceptible to inhibition by these compounds than the human G6PDH. The steroids also effectively kill cultured trypanosomes but not Leishmania and may be interesting leads for the development chemotherapeutic agents.

Headline: five different fatty acyl CoA synthetase isoenzymes
Content: Fatty acyl CoA synthetase (FACS). There are four tandemly linked facs genes with different chain length specificities present on chromosome 9 and a separate facs5 (or long chain acs5 or lacs5) on chromosome 10 (FACS1, Tb09.160.2770; FACS2, Tb09.160.2780; FACS3,Tb09.160.2810; FACS4, Tb09.160.2840; LACS5 Tb927.10.3260). Trypanosomes utilize enormous amounts of myristate to remodel the GPI anchor on the VSG that forms their surface coat. The substrate for remodeling is myristoyl-CoA which is formed by FACS.Facs 1,  3 and 4, have strong activity towards myristic acid,  while FACS2, favors shorter fatty acids. Most likely FACS3, the predominant FACS in bloodstream form trypanosomes, whose recombinant protein has the highest activity toward myristate (Jiang et al., 2001;PMID:11685899) plays a major role in myristate activation. FACS3 and FACS4 have both been identified in bloodstream form preparations (Jiang et al.2004, PMID:15287596).

Headline: Aspartate aminotransferase, two isoenzymes: mASAT and cASAT, the latter with functions in aromatic amino acid and methionine metabolism
Content:
Aspartate aminotransferase. There are two homologous isoenzymes, one (Tb11.02.2740) is the mitochondrial mASAT, while the other ( Tb10.70.3710) is the cytosolic cASAT. cASAT is constitutively expressed in T. brucei, whereas mASAT is down-regulated in the bloodstream forms (Marciano et al., 2008:PMID:18602174. The cASAT fulfils important functions other than than in aspartate transamination, as well. The enzymes of the classical pathway for aromatic amino-acid oxidation are missing in T. brucei. While there is a tyrosine amino transferase in T. cruzi, this enzyme is absent in T. brucei and has been replaced by a broad specificity cytosolic aspartate aminotransferase (cASAT, Tb10.70.3710, Marciano et al., 2008 PMID:18602174; Vernal et al., 1998;PMID:9851609) that is active on aromatic amino acids and on methionine (see: methionine salvage). Together with an aromatic alpha-hydroxy acid dehydrogenase (AHDH, Tb11.01.3040), an enzyme of the cytosolic malate dehydrogenase (MDH) family, but without MDH activity (Cazzulo-Franke et al., 1999;PMID:10583384), these two enzymes are responsible for the catabolism of aromatic amino acids to the corresponding aromatic hydroxyacid derivatives. This AHDH fulfils an important role in the re-oxidation of cytoplasmic NADH. Since the T. brucei AHDH is not expressed in the bloodstream form (Aranda et al., 2006;PMID:16321390) it provides a plausible explanation for the accumulation and secretion of large amounts of aromatic ketoacids in the blood of infected animals (El Sawalhy et al., 1998:PMID:9645841).  
The Crithidia fasciculata ASAT has been shown to be able to function as a methionine transaminase as well (Berger et al., 1998; PMID: 8633027).

Headline: methionine salvage pathway
Content:
This pathway, present in bacteria, plants and mammals, includes 8 enzymes involved in the formation from methionine or S-adenosylmethionine, which is required for polyamine synthesis. The resulting S-methyl-5-thioadenosine is reconverted to methionine in pathway similar, but not identical, to the "methionine salvage I" pathway of MetaCyc (http://metacyc.org/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-4361) comprising the following enzymes : 
1) s-adenosylmethionine synthase or methionine adenosyltransferase (Tb927.6.4840,Tb927.6.4850,Tb927.6.4860,Tb927.6.4870,Tb927.6.4880,Tb927.6.4890,Tb927.6.4900,Tb927.6.4910,Tb927.6.4920)
2) S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (Tb927.6.4410), regulatory subunit (Tb927.6.4470)
3) spermidine synthase (Tb09.v1.0380)
4) methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (Tb927.7.7040)
5) methylthioribose-1-phosphate isomerase|translation initiation factor 2 subunit (Tb11.01.2780)
6) methylthioribulose-1-phosphate dehydratase/enolase-phosphatase E1 (bifunctional)(not detected in T. brucei and T. cruzi, but present in Leishmania, crithidia, phytomonas and leptomonas)
7) 1,2-dihydroxy-3-keto-5-methylthiopentene dioxygenase or spontaneous (Tb927.4.360)
8) aspartate aminotransferase, putative broad specificity (methionine transaminase)(Tb10.70.3710)
Interestingly, apart from Berger et al.(1996,PMID 8633027) who characterized the last enzyme of the pathway, nobody has sofar characterized this pathway in any detail in trypanosomatids. The overall reaction of this salvage cycle is:
putrescine + amino acid + ATP + O2 ¿> spermidine + 2-oxoacid + 3 phosphate + adenine + CO2 + formate
PubMed Titles: Aromatic amino acid transamination and methionine recycling in trypanosomatids.

Headline: Glucose transporter is encoded by a tandemly arranged multigene family
Content:
The T. brucei glucose transporter is encoded by a tandemly arranged multigene family. It is composed of two homologous
groups of genes called THT1 (six copies) and THT2 (five copies) (Bringaud and Baltz, 1993;PMID: 8423781.(THT1: Tb927.10.8440 THT1B,Tb927.10.8450 THT1E, Tb927.10.8460, Tb927.10.8470, Tb927.10.8480 and THT2: Tb927.10.8490, Tb927.10.8500, Tb927.10.8510, Tb927.10.8520, Tb927.10.8530 THT2A). The THT1 genes encode the trypanosome bloodstream-form transporter. This THT1-encoded transport system for glucose differs from the human erythrocyte-type glucose transporter by its moderate sensitivity to cytochalasin B and its capacity to transport D-fructose. The expression of these genes is life-cycle stage dependent. THT1 is expressed in bloodstream forms and has a relative low affinity for glucose, while THT2 has a relatively high affinity for glucose and is expressed in procyclic trypanosomes (Barrett et al., 1995;PMID: 8554506). In addition there is a single copy of a divergent glucose transporter on chromosome 4 (Tb927.4.2290) that differs by 65% from the THT1 and THT2 transporters. The THT1 glucose transporter has been shown to be the most important rate-limiting step in the glycolytic pathway (Ter Kuile and Opperdoes, 1991 ;PMID: 1985967; Bakker er al., 1999; PMID: 10468568), and has been suggested to be an excellent target for drug development (Bringaud and Baltz, 1993;PMID: 8423781).

Headline: NDH2, a nitroreductase as well?

The function of this alternative NADH dehydrogenase in cell metabolism has been investigated (see Fang and Beattie, 2003;PMID:12615338; Verner et al., 2012;PMID:23111000). The enzyme is located on the outside of the mitochondrial inner membrane and is involved in the oxidation of cytosolic NADH. Wilkinson et al. (2008; PMID:18367671) have characterized a similar activity (Tb927.7.7230) as a nitroreductase of type I that is able to activate nifurtimox and benznidazole producing toxic metabolites responsible for the mode of action of these trypanocidal drugs. This enzyme also uses NADH as substrate and ubiquinone as acceptor.

Headline: Assembly of TbBILBO1 revealed by biochemical/biophysical studies
Content: We have carefully examined TbBILBO1 by systematically looking into its 4 structural modules using various biochemical/biophysical methods. Our data suggest that the protein first forms an antiparalell dimer by its C-terminal coiled-coil domain(CCD), and then the linear dimers are interconnected via the antiparalell interaction via the short leucine zipper at the very C-terminus of the CCD, which generates a long filament. Such filaments further assemble into a bundle via lateral interactions along the filaments. The two N-terminal globular domains (i.e. NTD & EFh) are not essential for filament assembly but may regulate such a process.
PubMed Titles: Assembly mechanism of Trypanosoma brucei BILBO1, a multidomain cytoskeletal protein.

Headline: A new TET-JBP family
Content: J -binding proteins 1 and 2 (JBP1 and 2) have become members of the new TET-JBP family of 2-oxoglutarate-Fe(II) dioxygenases (Tahiliani et al., 2009). Using the thymidine dioxygenase (thymidine hydroxylase ) domain of JBP1/2 as the start for a database search, Iyer et al. (Cell Cycle , in press) identified 3 JBP-related sequences in mammalian DNA (TET1-3 ), and demonstrated that TET1 can convert methylC in DNA into hydroxymethylC (hmC) both in mammalian cells and in vitro (Tahiliani et al., 2009). The purified enzyme is completely dependent on Fe(II) and 2-oxoglutarate for hmC synthesis. The hmC is naturally present in DNA of ES cells and has also been found in an independent study in brain cells (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009).

Headline: five different SOD isoenzymes
Content:
Superoxide dismutase
In the T. brucei genome there are five superoxide dismutase (SOD) genes: soda (Tb927.5.3350), sodb1 (Tb11.01.7550), sodb2 (Tb11.01.6660), sodc (Tb11.01.7480) and a as yet uncharacterized sod sequence (Tb927.6.4030) with a predicted mitochondrial targeting signal. Four of the five genes have been cloned, sequenced, and overexpressed in Escherichia coli and shown to encode active dimeric Fe-containing SOD isozymes. Subcellular localization using GFP-fusion proteins in procyclic insect trypomastigotes shows that TbSODB1 is mainly cytosolic, with a minor glycosomal component, TbSODB2 is mainly glycosomal with some activity in the cytosol, and TbSODA and TbSODC are both mitochondrial isozymes. Phylogenetic analysis has shown that the trypanosomatid SODs have all been acquired by more than one event of horizontal gene transfer,followed by events of gene duplication (Dufernez et al., 2005;PMID: 16413404)
Categories: Name/Product, Function, Expression, Sequence, Gene Model

Headline: This subunit is MED-T1 and not MED1
Content:
Mediator subunits between yeast and humans are conserved enough to identify orthologous subunits. These were named MED1-MED31. However, there is no sequence similarity between trypanosome and yeast/human mediator subunits. The trypanosome mediator complex was identified as such by structural and functional analyses alone. Thus, MED-T1 is likely not the orthologue of human/yeast MED1 as the current annotation suggests and this is true for all nine MED-T subunits.
MED1-9 annotations need to be changed to MED-T1-9 to not be misleading.

Headline: Glycosomal enzyme and potential target for drug development
Content: UDP-galactose 4'-epimerase in T. brucei and T. cruzi have a potential C-terminal glycosomal targeting signal (PTS1, -TKL and -SNL, respectively), while the L. major orthologue LmjF33.2300 udp-glc 4'-epimerase has a potential N-terminal glycosomal targeting signal (PTS2). This, together with the fact that the galactokinases from both T. cruzi and L. major have a potential PTS1 (-GKL,-SNL and -SKL) is suggestive of a glycosomal localization of these galactose-pathway enzymes (the latter enzyme is absent from T. brucei, though). The T. brucei galactose synthesis pathway is a potential therapeutic target. Although galactose is essential for T. brucei survival, the parasite lacks the transporters required to intake galactose from the environment. UDP-galactose 4'-epimerase (TbGalE) is responsible for the epimerization of UDP-glucose to UDP-galactose and is therefore of great interest to medicinal chemists. Crystal structure is available (Shaw et al.2003; PMID:12615316)
PubMed Titles: High-resolution crystal structure of Trypanosoma brucei UDP-galactose 4'-epimerase: a potential target for structure-based development of novel trypanocides.

Headline: Fumarate hydratase has multiple isoenzymes
Content:
Fumarase
In Trypanosomatids there are two fumarate hydratases which differ by 40% (they are both of Class I). One is mitochondrial (Tb11.02.2700) with clear mtochondrial transit sequence and the other is glycosomal/cytosolic (Tb927.3.4500) with a non-canonical PTS1. There is considerable variation in the glycosomal PTS1 (SKL, EQL, QQL, AKLV(tb). The T. brucei  enzyme is the most abundant enzyme in the glycosomal proteome of procyclics and is not expressed in the bloodstream form (Vertommen et al., 2008;PMID:18242729). The leishmania homologue increases in abundance by two-fold in the amastigote as compared to the promastigote (Rozenzweig,2008;PMID: 17884972).
PubMed Titles: Retooling Leishmania metabolism: from sand fly gut to human macrophage. | Differential expression of glycosomal and mitochondrial proteins in the two major life-cycle stages of Trypanosoma brucei.

Headline: TbPIF1, a Trypanosoma brucei Mitochondrial DNA Helicase, Is Essential for Kinetoplast Minicircle Replication
Content:
TbPIF1, functions in minicircle replication. RNA interference
(RNAi) of TbPIF1 causes a growth defect and kinetoplast
DNA loss. Minicircle replication intermediates decrease
during RNAi, and there is an accumulation of multiply interlocked,
covalently closed minicircle dimers (fraction U). In
studying the significance of fraction U, we found that this species
also accumulates during RNAi of mitochondrial topoisomerase
II. These data indicate that one function of TbPIF1 is
an involvement, together with topoisomerase II, in the segregation
of minicircle progeny.
PubMed Titles: TbPIF1, a Trypanosoma brucei mitochondrial DNA helicase, is essential for kinetoplast minicircle replication.

Headline: TbPIF2, one of six mitochondrial helicases,  controls kinetoplast maxicircle replication
Content: TbPIF2 is essential for maxicircle replication. Maxicircle abundance is controlled by TbPIF2 level, as RNAi of this helicase caused maxicircle loss, and its overexpression caused a 3- to 6-fold increase in maxicircle abundance. This regulation of maxicircle level is mediated by the TbHslVU protease. Previous experiments demonstrated that RNAi knockdown of TbHslVU dramatically increased abundance of minicircles and maxicircles, presumably because a positive regulator of their synthesis escaped proteolysis and allowed synthesis to continue. Here, we found that TbPIF2 level increases following RNAi of the protease. Therefore, this helicase is a TbHslVU substrate and an example of a positive regulator, thus providing a molecular mechanism for controlling maxicircle replication.
PubMed Titles: Trypanosomes have six mitochondrial DNA helicases with one controlling kinetoplast maxicircle replication.

Headline: An enzyme of the pentose-phosphate shunt
Content:
Ribose-5-phosphate isomerase
This enzyme is part of the pentose-phosphate pathway. Both bloodstream forms and procyclic insect stages contain glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.49), 6-phosphogluconolactonase (EC 3.1.1.31), 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.44), ribose-5-phosphate isomerase (EC 5.3.1.6) and transaldolase (EC 2.2.1.2). However, ribulose-5-phosphate 3'-epimerase (EC 5.1.3.1) and transketolase (EC 2.2.1.1) activities are detectable only in procyclic forms (Cronin et al, 1989, PMID:2924907). Enzymes of this pathway have been detected both in the cytosol and in glycosomes
PubMed Titles: The enzymes of the classical pentose phosphate pathway display differential activities in procyclic and bloodstream forms of Trypanosoma brucei.

Headline: CRK9 is important for gene expression and mitosis/cytokinesis
Content:
- CRK9 ablation led to cytokinesis/mitosis defects in procyclic form (PF) T. brucei.
- CRK9 is essential for the viability of PFs and bloodstream forms.
- CRK9 silencing inhibited the first step of spliced leader (SL) trans splicing, led to an accumulation SL RNA with a hypomethylated cap (predominantly cap0), and caused phosphorylation loss of RPB1, the largest subunit of RNA pol II.
- CRK9 forms an active kinase complex with CYC12 (Tb927.10.9160) and the CRK9 associated protein CRK9AP (Tb927.3.4170).
- CRK9 was validated as a drug target in the mouse.
- CRK9 appears to be a functional homolog of human CDK11.

Headline: DCL2
Content: Contributes to the biogenesis of siRNAs from retroposons. Authors propose a model whereby TbDCL2 fuels the T. brucei nuclear RNAi pathway and TbDCL1 patrols the cytoplasm.

Headline: Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, also known as diaphorase and menadione reductase
Content: Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, also known as diaphorase and menadione reductase, is an essential cofactor of several mitochondrial multienzyme complexes: the E3 component of the alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (2OGDH) and the H-protein of the glycine cleavage system. Due to the absence of PDH and 2OGDH in bloodstream forms the mitochondrial dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DHLDH) is believed to mislocalise to plasma membranes (Danson et al., 1987;PMID: 3663096). The distribution of DHLDH is over the whole surface of the membrane, including the flagellar pocket region, and the enzyme is not found in any other cellular fraction and a study of the latency of the enzyme suggests that it is located on the cytoplasmic surface of the plasma membrane (Jackman et al., 1990; PMID: 2226451). However, Krauth-Siegel and coworkers were only able to find the enzyme in the mitochondrion of both bloodstream and procyclic stages (personal communication). The substrate dihydrolipoamide (and also dihydrolipoic acid) form stable complexes with melarsen oxide, the active principle of the trypanocidal drug melarsoprol (Fairlamb et al., 1992; PMID: 1501642). The gene has been cloned and sequenced  (Else et al., 1993;PMID: 8444180). DHLDH is differentially expressed during transformation and has been demonstrated by immunofluorescence in stumpy and in procyclic forms (Tyler et al., 1997;PMID: 9364788; Breidbach et al., 2002; PMID: 12594963). RNAi and gene deletion has shown that DHLDH is an essential enzyme for both bloodstream and procyclic stages (Roldan et al. 2011; PMID: 21631607). Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase is also a constituent of the mitochondrial glycine cleavage system in bloodstream forms (Krauth-Siegel and coworkers, unpublished).

It has also been shown that dioxygen is required for the methionine salvage pathway. The aci-reductone dioxygenase that creates 2-keto-4-methylthiobutyrate (KMTB) has counterparts in many Bacteria and Eukarya, including in mammals. It seems to be absent from Archaea. Interestingly, the enzyme has two activities, depending on its metal co-factor. When iron is involved, the enzyme produces KMTB, the immediate precursor of methionine, together with formate. In contrast, when nickel is involved, carbon monoxide is produced in addition to formate, together with 3-methylthiopropionate. The counterpart of the dioxygenase is not known in organisms that live under anaerobic growth conditions. (See Sekowska et al 2004;   PMID: 15102328

Headline: Complex III, or bc1 complex
Content: Ubiquinone cytochrome c oxidoreductase or the respiratory chain complex iii consist of cytochrome b, Rieske iron sulphur protein, cytochrome c1 and core protein. Contrary to the enzymes from other eukaryotes the ubiquinone cytochrome c oxidoreductase or bc1 complex of T. brucei does not seem to play a role in superoxide production. Also the enzyme is resistant to myxothiazol and stigmatellin, two inhibitors of the bc1 complex . Since these compounds bind to the ubiquinol-oxidizing site of the bc1 complex this suggests that the bc1 complex of trypanosomes may differ significantly from bc1 complexes of other organisms (see: Fang and Beattie, 2003;PMID: 12781782). See also Tb927.4.4990

Headline: The genes of the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway
Content: All Trypanosomatidae including, T. brucei, synthesise pyrimidines de novo from glutamine, bicarbonate and aspartate. This involves five genes. Four of them are tandemly linked (Gao et al, 1999; PMID:9878395). Contrary to  the situation in mammals where the first three proteins of the pathway have been fused into a single gene encoding a multifunctional protein, in trypanosomatids the genes encoding glutamine-dependent carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase, aspartate carbamoyltransferase and dihydroorotase are separate. Dihydroorotate is oxidised by a cytosolic dihydroorotate dehydrogenase of bacterial origin and not by a mitochondrial oxidase as in all other eukaryotes. The enzyme utilises fumarate as electron acceptor. This situation is furthermore only found in yeast. The subsequent two steps of the pathawy are catalysed inside glycosomes by a bifunctional orotidine-5'-phosphate decarboxylase/orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (Hammond et al,1989; PMID:7274454), the genes of which have been fused to encode a bifunctional protein. Interestingly, this fusion occurred in the opposite direction to what is found in higher eukaryotes (Gao et al, 1999; PMID:9878395) and so far this reversed fusion is only shared with some cyanobacteria (Opperdoes and Michels 2007; PMID:17826337).
PubMed Titles: A novel location for two enzymes of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis in trypanosomes and Leishmania. | Horizontal gene transfer in trypanosomatids. | Novel organization and sequences of five genes encoding all six enzymes for de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis in Trypanosoma cruzi.

Interestingly, this fusion occurred in the opposite direction of what is found in higher eukaryotes (Gao et al, 1999; PMID:9878395) and so far this reversed fusion is only shared with some cyanobacteria (Opperdoes and Michels 2007; PMID:17826337). The two enzymatic activities have been localised to glycosomes (Hammond et al,1989; PMID:7274454) and the protein has been detected in glycosomal fractions of both bloodstream and procyclic insect stages (Vertommen et al., 2008;PMID:18242729)). The gene encodes a glycosome targeting signal of type one (PTS1) (Opperdoes and Szikora, 2006; PMID 16546274).

Headline: This enzyme is a dihydroorote dehydrogenase PYR4 (EC 1.3.98.1) (fumarate)
Content: The fourth enzyme of the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase or oxidase, is usually particulate, mitochondrial membrane enzyme and intimately connected to the respiratory chain, using quinone as electron acceptor (EC 1.3.5.2). However, in the Kinetoplastida there is an isofunctional enzyme, which is cytosolic and functions as a dehydrogenase (PYR4,Tb927.5.3830) rather than an oxidase. The gene is of bacterial origin and not homologous with the mitochondrial dihydroorotate oxidase of the other eukaryotes. Moreover the enzyme utilises fumarate as electron acceptor and therefore its EC number should be EC 1.3.98.1. While common to bacteria, this enzyme is not present in eukaryotes except in the Kinetoplastida and yeast. The T. brucei enzyme has been characterized, 3-D structures (e.g. 2B4G) are available and the enzyme has been validated as a potential drug target (Arakaki et al., 2008;PMID:18312275).

Headline: a family of 4 elongases
Content:
Fatty acid elongase: T. brucei has three fatty acid elongases  (Tb927.7.4160 or ELO3, Tb927.7.4170 or ELO2, Tb927.7.4180 or ELO1). The three tandemly repeated elongases differ by more than 50% and they have been shown by Lee et al.,2006; (PMID:16923389) to be involved in synthesis of myristic acid (C14) and longer fatty acids in bloodstream forms. They are associated with the ER (Englund, personal communication). Trypanosoma brucei, uses three elongases instead of type I or type II synthases for the synthesis of nearly all its fatty acids. The procyclic form requires synthesis of stearate (C18), whereas the bloodstream form needs myristate (C14). Trypanosome fatty acid synthesis is modular, with
ELO1 converting C4 to C10, ELO2 extending C10 to C14, and ELO3 elongating C14 to 
C18. In blood, ELO3 downregulation favors myristate synthesis, whereas low
concentrations of exogenous fatty acids in cultured parasites cause upregulation 
of the entire pathway, allowing the parasite to adapt to different environments. There is also an elongase for very long chain fatty acids (ELO4 or Tb927.5.4530).
PubMed Titles: Fatty acid synthesis by elongases in trypanosomes.

Headline: This is NOT the functional orthologue of Dcp2.
Content: This nudix domain protein (formerly Nudix4) has very low similarity to Dcp2 and its vitro decapping activity is poor, when a fully mature mRNA cap is used (PMID 26038549). RNAi depletion has no effect on growth, mRNA levels or change in poly(A) tail length (PMID 28628654). The protein was not identified in any mRNA related screening experiments that I am aware off. Thus, at the current time there is no evidence for this protein to be the major mRNA decapping enzyme and thus the functional orthologue to Dcp2. This does not exclude that it plays a role RNA cap quality surveillance, or, perhaps is the decapping enzyme of a small subset of mRNAs. The functional orthologue to Dcp2 is the ApaH like phosphatase ALPH1 (Tb927.6.640), PMID 28628654.

Headline: Threonine dehyrogenase, a result of an event of lateral gene transfer
Content: The enzyme is only present in trypanosomes (T.brucei, T.cruzi, T.vivax and T. congolense, not in Leishmania, Crithidia and Phytomonas. This pathway of threonine catabolism has been described for T. brucei procyclics by Lindstead et al. (1977; PMID: 925677). The two additional enzymes of the pathway: aminoacetone synthase and acetyl CoA hydrolase, were also not found in the leishmania. The enzyme has been localized to the mitochondrion (Opperdoes et al., 1981;PMID: 6801509) and TargetP predicts the presence of a mitochondrial signal peptide.  Enzyme is expressed in both procyclics and bloodstream forms (Mazet et al., 2013). Phylogenetic analysis suggests that the enzyme is of bacterial origin. For a tree see: http://www.icp.ucl.ac.be/~opperd/jpgs/226.m00595.jpg. In the other trypanosomatids threonine degration takes place via a pathway where the enzyme L-threonine aldolase (EC 4.1.2.5) cleaves threonine directly into glycine and acetaldehyde.

Headline: A unique mRNA decapping complex in trypanosomes

Just like ALPH1, all ALPH1-associated proteins localise to a structure at the posterior pole of the cell, anterior to the microtubule plus ends. The ALPH1 N-terminus is not required for viability in culture, but essential for posterior pole localisation. The C-terminus, in contrast, is required for localisation to all RNA granule types, as well as for dimerisation and interactions with XRNA and the CMGC kinase.

Headline: C-1-tetrahydrofolate synthase, dhch1 gene, or N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase/N5,N10-methenyltetrahydrofolate cyclohydrolase (DHCH1)
Content: Humans possess a cytosolic trifunctional C-1-tetrahydrofolate synthase with DHCH and formyltetrahydrofolate ligase (FTL) activities, in addition to a mitochondrial bifunctional DHCH and monofunctional FTL. All trypanosomatids possess this dehydrogenase and cyclohydrolase activity with a cytosolic bifunctional enzyme (DHCH1). In Leishmania major and Trypanosoma cruzi a separate enzyme catalyzes the FTL reaction but this enzyme is absent in T. brucei (Opperdoes and Coombs, 2007; PMID:17320480; Vickers et al., 2009; PMID:19450731)). Leishmania possesses an additional putative mitochondrial enzyme (DHCH2) that shares between 27 and 31% sequence identity with DHCH1. The cytosolic DHCH1 activity appears essential in L. major since knockouts of the disomic copies were not possible without ectopic expression of FTL to provide an alternative route to N10-formyltetrahydrofolate (Murta et al, 2009; PMID:19183277). A crystal structure of the L. major DHCH1 is available (PDB code 4A26; Eadsforth et al., 2012; PMID:22108435)

Headline: MCM-BP funciton
Content: Part of Abstract: A previously published genetic screen identified the T. brucei MCM-BP, which interacts with subunits of MCM helicase, as a protein whose downregulation results in the loss of transcriptional silencing at subtelomeric loci. Here, I show that TbMCM-BP is required for DNA replication and transcription. TbMCM-BP depletion causes a significant reduction of replicating cells in S phase and genome-wide impairments of replication origin activation. Moreover, levels of sense and antisense transcripts increase at boundaries of PTUs in the absence of TbMCM-BP. TbMCM-BP is also important for transcriptional repression of the specialized subtelomeric PTUs, the Bloodstream-form Expression-Sites (BESs), which house the major antigenic determinant (the Variant Surface Glycoprotein, VSG gene) as well as TbORC1 binding sites. Overall, this study reveals that TbMCM-BP, a replication initiation protein, also guides the initiation, termination and directionality of transcription.

Headline: Only one thiolase in T.brucei
Content: T. brucei has one thiolase isoenzyme of the SCP2-thiolase type, whereas the TFE-thiolase was also found in T.cruzi and Leishmania spp., and the AB-thiolase only in T. cruzi. The T. brucei protein has both a predicted N-terminal mitochondrial signal peptide and a C-terminal candidate type 1 peroxisomal-targeting signal (PTS1) for sorting it into glycosomes. It has been expressed in Escherichia coli and characterized. Transcripts of this thiolase were detected in both bloodstream- and procyclic-form trypanosomes, but the protein was found only in the procyclic form. However experimentally, only a mitochondrial localization was found for both procyclic trypanosomes grown with glucose and cells cultured with amino acids as an energy source. Headline: sterol01/ Erg10: Acetoacetyl CoA thiolase (EC 2.3.1.9) is absent in T. brucei
Content:
sterol01: Acetoacetyl CoA thiolase EC 2.3.1.9
This enzyme is homologous to the yeast Erg10 acetoacetyl CoA thiolase, an enzyme of the ergosterol biosynthetic pathway. This thiolase is involved in the synthesis of hydroxymethylglutaryl-Coenzyme A (HMGCoA) required for sterol synthesis. it is normally present in the cytosol. The isoenzyme involved in ketone body formation is a mitochondrial enzyme (3-keto acyl-CoA thiolase; Tb927.8.2540). The Erg10 homologue is absent in T. brucei. Apparently in T. brucei acetoacetyl CoA cannot be formed from acetate by condensation of two acetyl-CoA as in other organisms. However, there is an alternative route to form HMGCoA from the breakdown of leucine as has been demonstrated for Leishmania (Ginger et al 2001;PMID: 11148203) and T. brucei (Nes et al., 2012;PMID: 22176028).
PubMed Titles: The biosynthetic incorporation of the intact leucine skeleton into sterol by the trypanosomatid Leishmania mexicana. | Novel sterol metabolic network of Trypanosoma brucei procyclic and bloodstream forms.

Headline: TbPRI1:   A Mitochondrial DNA Primase Is Essential for Cell Growth and Kinetoplast DNA Replication in Trypanosoma brucei
Content:
A Trypanosoma brucei DNA primase gene, PRI1, that encodes a 70-kDa protein that localizes to the kinetoplast
and is essential for both cell growth and kinetoplast DNA replication. The expression of PRI1 mRNA is cyclic
and reaches maximum levels at a time corresponding to duplication of the kinetoplast DNA. A 3 -hydroxylterminated
oligoriboadenylate is synthesized on a poly(dT) template by a recombinant form of the PRI1 protein
and is subsequently elongated by DNA polymerase and added dATP. Poly(dA) synthesis is dependent on both
PRI1 protein and ATP and is inhibited by RNase H treatment of the product of PRI1 synthesis.

Headline: TbPIF5 is a Trypanosoma brucei mitochondrial DNA helicase involved in processing of minicircle Okazaki fragments
Content: TbPIF5 is a 5' to 3' DNA helicase. Together with other enzymes thought to be involved in Okazaki fragment processing, TbPIF5 localizes in vivo to the antipodal sites flanking the kDNA. Minicircles in wild type cells replicate unidirectionally as theta-structures and are unusual in that Okazaki fragments are not joined until after the progeny minicircles have segregated. We now report that overexpression of TbPIF5 causes premature removal of RNA primers and joining of Okazaki fragments on theta structures. Further elongation of the lagging strand is blocked, but the leading strand is completed and the minicircle progeny, one with a truncated H strand (ranging from 0.1 to 1 kb), are segregated. The minicircles with a truncated H strand electrophorese on an agarose gel as a smear. This replication defect is associated with kinetoplast shrinkage and eventual slowing of cell growth. We propose that TbPIF5 unwinds RNA primers after lagging strand synthesis, thus facilitating processing of Okazaki fragments.
PubMed Titles: TbPIF5 is a Trypanosoma brucei mitochondrial DNA helicase involved in processing of minicircle Okazaki fragments.

Headline: Binds to G-tracts
Content: Paper abstract: The authors studied the RNA binding specificity of the simplest T. brucei PPR protein (KRIPP11) using electrophoretic mobility shift assays, fluorescence anisotropy, circular dichroism spectroscopy, and in vitro selection. We found KRIPP11 to be an RNA binding protein with specificity for sequences of four or more consecutive guanosine residues (G-tracts). Such G-tracts are dramatically enriched in T. brucei mitochondrial transcripts that are destined for extensive uridine insertion/deletion editing but are not present in mRNAs following editing. We further found that the quadruplex oligoguanosine RNA conformation is preferentially recognized by KRIPP11 over other conformational forms, and is bound without disruption of the quadruplex structure. In combination with prior data demonstrating association of KRIPP11 with the small ribosomal subunit, these results suggest possible roles for KRIPP11 in bridging mRNA maturation and translation or in facilitating translation of unusual dual-coded open reading frames.
PubMed Titles: The 27 kDa Trypanosoma brucei Pentatricopeptide Repeat Protein is a G-tract Specific RNA Binding Protein.

Headline: MIC60 component of MICOS complex
Content: Abstract from paper: The mitochondrial contact site and cristae organization system (MICOS) is a multiprotein complex responsible for cristae formation. Even though cristae are found in all mitochondria capable of oxidative phosphorylation, only Mic10 and Mic60 appear to be conserved throughout eukaryotes. The remaining 4 or 5 known MICOS subunits are specific to the supergroup Opisthokonta, which includes yeast and mammals that are the only organisms in which this complex has been analyzed experimentally. We have isolated the MICOS from Trypanosoma brucei, a member of the supergroup Excavata that is profoundly diverged from opisthokonts. We show that it is required for the maintenance of the unique discoidal cristae that typify excavates, such as euglenids and kinetoplastids, the latter of which include trypanosomes. The trypanosome MICOS consists of 9 subunits, most of which are essential for normal growth. Unlike in opisthokonts, it contains two distinct Mic10 orthologs and an unconventional putative Mic60 that lacks a mitofilin domain.
PubMed Titles: The Diverged Trypanosome MICOS Complex as a Hub for Mitochondrial Cristae Shaping and Protein Import.

Headline: References for GIM5A and GIM5B, depletion phenotypes
Content:
Genes encoding the most abundant protein of the glycosomal membrane, GIM5, have been cloned and the protein characterized. Two genes, GIM5A and GIM5B, encode 26 kDa proteins. Although many microbody membrane proteins are conserved in evolution, the only homologues of GIM5 in the available databases are from the closely related kinetoplastids Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania. The N- and C-termini are conserved between the two genes, and between species, and are oriented towards the cytosol. They are separated by a short loop that is located between two transmembrane domains and shows almost no sequence conservation. This suggests that the N- and C-terminal domains are more important for function. GIM5 forms dimers in vivo. Overexpression of GIM5B inhibits growth, whereas depletion of GIM5 to below 10% of wild-type levels is very rapidly lethal.
Procyclic trypanosomes survive without GIM5A and with very low levels of GIM5B. The depleted cells have fewer glycosomes than usual and are osmotically fragile, which is a novel observation for a microbody defect. Thus trypanosomes require both GIM5B and PEX11 for the maintenance of normal glycosome numbers. Procyclic cells lacking GIM5A, like mouse cells partially defective in PEX11, have fewer ether-linked phospholipids, even when GIM5B levels are not reduced. Metabolite measurements on GIM5A/B-depleted bloodstream form trypanosomes suggested a change in the flux through the glycolytic pathway.
PubMed Titles: Depletion of GIM5 causes cellular fragility, a decreased glycosome number, and reduced levels of ether-linked phospholipids in trypanosomes. | An essential dimeric membrane protein of trypanosome glycosomes.
PubMed Authors: Voncken et al. | Maier et al.

Headline: 6PGDH is the result of an event of lateral gene transfer
Content:
6PGDH
A phylogenetic tree comprising 100 taxa shows that the trypanosomatid enzymes are closely related to the enzymes of Chlamydomonas reinhartii, and Prochlorococcus marinus (strain MIT 9313) and other cyanobacteria. This clustering gets over 70% bootstrap support. There are no other eukaryotic homologues with the first 100 best sequences in the database. This suggests that the gene was acquired by horizontal transfer. The L. mexicana enzyme has been cloned, sequenced and a structure is available (Gonzalez et al 2010; PMID:21160204)

Only one copy of each is present in the T. brucei genome database, but most other copies are present in telomeric expression sites on mini chromosomes carrying VSG genes as well. Each of the 20 ESs encodes a slightly different Tf-R; these differences strongly affect the binding affinity for Tfs of different hosts (Van Luenen et al., 2005; PMID: 16164555; Gerrits et al., 2002;PMID: 11814575).

Headline: Cytosolic localization in procyclic forms based on endogenous tagging
Content:
It has not been described as an acidocalcisomal protein.
Luginbuehl et al. (2011) performed the C-terminal endogenous tagging of TbrPPX in both procyclic and bloodstream forms. In procyclic forms, a diffuse cytosolic staining throughout the entire cell body was detected. In bloodstream forms, a punctate labeling was found. None of them colocalized with an acidocalcisome marker.
The TrypTag project (tryptag.org) has recently N-terminally tagged this protein and a cytosolic distribution was also detected in procyclic forms, corroborating the localization of TbrPPX from the work previously mentioned.
Thus the product description as an acidocalcisomal exopolyphosphatase has not been described in T. brucei.
PubMed Titles: The exopolyphosphatase TbrPPX1 of Trypanosoma brucei. | TrypTag.org: A Trypanosome Genome-wide Protein Localisation Resource.

Headline: mt-LAF3 is a pseudouridine synthase ortholog required for mitochondrial rRNA and mRNA gene expression
Content: mt-LAF3 is an ortholog of human and yeast mitochondrial PUS enzymes, and a mitoribosome assembly factor, but structural studies differ in their conclusion as to whether it has PUS catalytic activity. T. brucei cells that are conditionally null for mt-LAF3 expression and showed that mt-LAF3 loss is lethal and disrupts mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm). Loss of mt-LAF3 dramatically decreases levels of mitochondrial 12S and 9S rRNAs. Decreases in mitochondrial mRNA levels were also observed, including differential effects on edited vs. pre-edited mRNAs, indicating that mt-LAF3 is required for mitochondrial rRNA and mRNA processing, including of edited transcripts.

Headline: Three AK isoenzymes
Content:
Arginine kinase (AK)
The enzyme is involved in the formation of high energy arginine-phosphate, which may replace carnitine-phosphate as an energy store. There are three tandemly linked arginine kinases in T. brucei (AK1,Tb09.160.4560; AK2,Tb09.160.4570 and AK3,Tb09.160.4590). They differ at their N- and C-termini, and are otherwise between 98 and 94% identical. AK1 is present in the flagellum, AK2 carries a PTS and has been detected in glycosomes of bloodforms and procyclics by proteomic analysis and immunofluorescence microscopy, and AK3 is cytosolic (Vertommen et al., 2007; PMID:18242729; Voncken et al., 2013;PMID:23776565). There are two AKs in T. cruzi and none in L. major, probably because of the presence of the arginine-consuming enzyme, arginase, only present in Leishmania. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that Kinetoplastids' arginine kinase was acquired, during evolution, from the arthropod vectors by horizontal gene transfer (Canepa et al., 2011; PMID: 21624495)
PubMed Titles: Differential expression of glycosomal and mitochondrial proteins in the two major life-cycle stages of Trypanosoma brucei. | Arginine kinase in Phytomonas, a trypanosomatid parasite of plants. | The phosphoarginine energy-buffering system of trypanosoma brucei involves multiple arginine kinase isoforms with different subcellular locations.

Headline: Functions of DRBD3 and DRBD4
Content:
Paper abstract: Trypanosomatid genomes encode for numerous proteins containing an RNA recognition motif (RRM), but the function of most
of these proteins in mRNA metabolism is currently unknown. Here, we report the function of two such proteins that we have
named PTB1 and PTB2, which resemble the mammalian polypyrimidine tract binding proteins (PTB). RNAi silencing of these
factors indicates that both are essential for life. PTB1 and PTB2 reside mostly in the nucleus, but are found in the cytoplasm, as
well. Microarray analysis performed on PTB1 and PTB2 RNAi silenced cells indicates that each of these factors differentially
affects the transcriptome, thus regulating a different subset of mRNAs. PTB1 and PTB2 substrates were categorized
bioinformatically, based on the presence of PTB binding sites in their 59 and 39 flanking sequences. Both proteins were shown
to regulate mRNA stability. Interestingly, PTB proteins are essential for trans-splicing of genes containing C-rich polypyrimidine
tracts. PTB1, but not PTB2, also affects cis-splicing. The specificity of binding of PTB1 was established in vivo and in vitro using a
model substrate. This study demonstrates for the first time that trans-splicing of only certain substrates requires specific factors
such as PTB proteins for their splicing. The trypanosome PTB proteins, like their mammalian homologs, represent multivalent
RNA binding proteins that regulate mRNAs from their synthesis to degradation.
PubMed Titles: Multiple roles for polypyrimidine tract binding (PTB) proteins in trypanosome RNA metabolism.

Headline: MASP structure, expression and localization
Content: The predicted mucin-associated surface proteins (MASPs) are characterized by highly conserved N- and C-terminal domains and a strikingly variable and repetitive central region. Masp transcripts vary in size, are preferentially expressed during the trypomastigote stage and contain highly conserved 5¿ and 3¿ untranslated regions.  Immunofluorescence assays using antibodies generated against a MASP peptide reveals that the expression of particular MASPs at the cell membrane is limited to subsets of the parasite population. Western blots of phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C (PI-PLC)-treated parasites suggest that MASP may be GPI-anchored.
PubMed Titles: Genomic organization and expression profile of the mucin-associated surface protein (masp) family of the human pathogen Trypanosoma cruzi.

Headline: Putative functions
Content: No biological function has yet been assigned to peptidases of the M32 family. Nevertheless, microarray experiments on the hyperthermophilic archaeon P. furiosus suggest that M32 peptidases may be involved in the utilization of peptides and proteins for nutrition in this organism, since the relative transcript levels of the ORF PF0456 (coding for an M32 peptidase) are up-regulated 2.6-fold when cells are grown in media containing peptides as the primary carbon source compared with those grown in maltose. Additional experiments performed on Bacillus subtilis knockout for the YpwA gene have shown that the enzyme is not essential for growth in glucose medium. Notably, this mutant showed improved growth in terms of rate and yield of biomass formation. Additional clues about the possible roles of these enzymes can be derived from the analysis of the crystal structure of PfuCP. This analysis revealed that the enzyme has a fold similar to those of ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme), ACE2, neurolysin and TOP (thimet oligopeptidase), all of which are zinc metallopeptidases with no detectable sequence similarity to M32 peptidases. Whereas ACE is a crucial regulator of the renin¿angiotensin system, converting the inactive decapeptide angiotensin I into the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, many biologically active peptides could be hydrolysed by ACE2. TOP has been implicated in the metabolism of a number of small peptides in the central nervous system, and recent studies have also demonstrated that this enzyme is primarily responsible for degrading peptides released from proteasomes, thereby limiting the extent of antigen presentation by MHC class I molecules. Thus we can speculate that a major role of the TcMCPs might be the degradation of peptides, such as those produced by the proteasomes, in the cytosol. However, a possible role in the processing of proteins and small regulatory peptides cannot be excluded at present.
PubMed Titles: Two metallocarboxypeptidases from the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi belong to the M32 family, found so far only in prokaryotes.

Headline: TcTASV
Content: T. cruzi trypomastogote alanine- serine- and valine-rich proteins (TcTASV) are a T. cruzi gene family characterized by highly conserved N- and C-terminal domains. The central region is variable and 3 sub-families (A, B and C) can be predicted. TcTASVs have no orthologues in other trypanosomatids, contained conserved 5¿ and 3¿ untranslated regions and are preferentially expressed in trypomastigotes (demostrated for TcTASV-A and TcTAV-C). Labelling of live parasites and detection by flow cytometry suggests that TcTASV-C are present at the cell membrane in CL-Brener and RA strains, but expressed in a limited subset of the parasite population (also confirmed by immunofluorescence assays). TcTASV-C are also secreted to the medium by cell-derived trypomastigotes.

Headline: Trypanosoma cruzi arginine kinase
Content: Arginine kinase (ATP:arginine phosphotransferase; EC 2.7.3.3) catalyze the reversible transphosphorylation between N-phospho-L-arginine and ATP (Ellington 2001). We have demonstrated the presence of an arginine kinase-mediated phosphagen system in Trypanosoma cruzi and Trypanosoma brucei (Pereira et al. 1999, 2000, 2002). Overexpression of T. cruzi arginine kinase improves the capability of transfectant parasites to grow and survive under nutritional and pH stress conditions (Pereira et al. 2003). These phenomena have been also observed when a heterologous arginine kinase was expressed in organisms lacking any kind of phosphagen kinase, such as yeast and bacteria (Canonaco et al. 2002, 2003). In addition, T. cruzi epimastigotes treated with hydrogen peroxide showed a time-dependent increase in arginine kinase expression suggesting the participation of this phosphagen system in oxidative stress responses (Miranda et al. 2006).
PubMed Titles: Trypanosoma cruzi arginine kinase characterization and cloning. A novel energetic pathway in protozoan parasites.

Headline: Myb-M: transcription factor that is necessary and sufficient to drive male fate

Conditional overexpression of the Myb-M protein drives all parasites to a male fate during the asexual cycle (at any time) and conditional deletion of Myb-M ablates the formation of male gamonts.

Headline: Expression and regulation of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum necrosis and ethylene-inducing peptides (NEPs).
Content: Successful host colonization by necrotrophic plant pathogens requires the induction of plant cell death to provide the nutrients needed for infection establishment and progression. We have cloned two genes encoding necrosis and ethylene-inducing peptides from Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, which we named SsNep1 and SsNep2. The peptides encoded by these genes induce necrosis when expressed transiently in tobacco leaves. SsNep1 is expressed at a very low level relative to SsNep2 during infection. The expression of SsNep2 was induced by contact with solid surfaces and occurred in both the necrotic zone and at the leading margin of the infection. SsNep2 expression was dependent on calcium and cyclic adenosine monophosphate signalling, as compounds affecting these pathways reduced or abolished SsNep2 expression coincident with a partial or total loss of virulence.
PubMed Titles: Expression and regulation of Sclerotinia sclerotiorum necrosis and ethylene-inducing peptides (NEPs).
